data.abstractNote: In fall 2020, the excavations division of the Directorate of Antiquities (DGAMS) undertook excavations in the Byzantine church in the al-Madinah neighbourhood, in old Hama (Epiphania of Apamene), which has been partly known since the 1980s and 1990s. The old excavations, led by A. Zaqzouq, uncovered two buildings, including a basilica with sidewalks and narthex, and its annex rooms dated by inscriptions from between 412 and 416. The floor of this religious complex is paved with mosaics with geometric patterns, except one with a figured scene. Above, a second building was paved with slabs. It dates back to the Middle Ages, and may have been a church according to M. Piccirillo. The recent excavations by the DGAMS aimed at clearing the area and identify the limits of the building. They uncovered several architectural pieces and new mosaics in the central nave and in the annex rooms. These mosaics bear various, fine geometric patterns, some of them unique in the region, as well as biblical quotes in Greek. These recent discoveries confirm the special status of this religious complex, especially in the Paleochristian period, and give a rare testimony on the Byzantine bishopric of Epiphania of Apamene.

Gregory of Nazianzus (329-389), who was functioning as bishop in the capital city of Constantinople, responded to the Arian challenge, particularly strong in that city, in five orations (27-31 in the collection of his orations) preached about 380, commonly called the Theological Orations. These are the foremost distillation of his thought on the Christological questions relating to the implications of professing belief in a Son consubstantial with the Heavenly Father, as well as his chief battleground with the contentions of those tending to side with Arius.
Ephraem's two collections, the hymns and sermons On the Faith are the fruit of this same struggle. The sermons are thought to have been composed while he was in Nisibis (i.e. before 363) while the hymns are thought to stem from the last decade of his life which was spent in Edessa (363-373). This chronological profile of his works against the Arian viewpoint shows that the question was of interest to Ephraem over a period of time. It also makes clear that these two collections of pieces were produced very near in time to Gregory's orations.
The purpose of this study is to set these two very important works more firmly in their contemporary settings and to discover the extent of the similarity between the methods and content of their arguments, always with attention to their context in the period leading up to the Council of Constantinople (381 AD).
Ephraem's treatment of Scripture and his theological contribution have received very little attention. A comparative study is long overdue and will offer a unique picture of the true state of the Church's intellectual life at a crucial juncture in Christian history. In fact, this study shows a considerable congruency between the arguments offered by these writers and should provide a strong case for the removal of Ephraem from the theological ghetto where he has too often languished and his reintroduction into the scholarly picture of the Arian Controversy.

data.title: The Concept of Rest in the Greek Acts of Thomas
data.abstractNote: Rest is an important soteriological and christological concept in the third century apocryphal Acts of Thomas. The forty-five references to rest (ἀνάπαυσις and its cognates) mark rest as a significant theme of the work. This article provides an analysis of the use of ἀνάπαυσις in the Greek Acts of Thomas. Rest is a rich and multifaceted motif that expresses both present experience and future hope. It is an attribute of Christ but also a benefit of being in union with Christ. Rest, achieved through rigorous “holiness” (abstinence, especially from sex), is synonymous with salvation. The Acts of Thomas’ understanding of rest is rooted in Jewish rest tradition, which the author/compiler has christianized and enriched with an ascetical emphasis that is characteristic of Syriac spirituality.
